newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus ghost town sleeps amid growing tension.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus ghost town sleeps amid growing tension.

text.p: Little stirred on Thursday on the empty streets of a ghost town that is a key pressure point in the deepening dispute between Greeks and Turks on the divided island of Cyprus.
Magpies picked their way over broken glass on cracked pavements and stray cats wary of humans darted through the grotesquely overgrown gardens of abandoned villas.

The sign on a post box says the next mail collection will be at 6.15 a.m. But the postman never comes. He and the resort town's 60,000 other Greek Cypriot residents fled in the face of advancing Turkish troops on August 16-17 in 1974, leaving Varosha uninhabited and suspended in time ever since.

A rusty crane towering over a half-built hotel still holds blocks of concrete in its clutches. Turkish officers and their families are now the only ones who bathe in the turquoise sea off the town's long, sandy beach.
But Varosha's eerie quiet may not last for long.

The Turkish Cypriot breakaway state, recognised only by Ankara, has threatened to settle civilians in Varosha in retaliation if Greek Cypriots deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles as planned next year. Some Turkish nationalists hope to take over Varosha, known in Turkish as Maras, before then.

"It is my personal belief that we should start opening Maras as soon as they begin paying the first installments for the missiles," said Turkish Cypriot official Serdar Denktash, influential son of the community's veteran leader, Rauf.
Any Turkish settlement of Varosha would outrage the Greek Cypriot administration in the south, regarded internationally as the island's legitimate government.
There are fears the two communities are closer to all out conflict now than at any time since Turkey invaded Cyprus 23 years ago in response to a Greek Cypriot coup.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned recently that tension in Cyprus could suck Greece and Turkey into war.
"It's a real tinderbox," said a Western diplomat in Ankara. "A stupid little incident on the Green Line could lead to God knows what," he said.
An imminent threat to peace was averted this week when Turkish far-rightists postponed a plan to storm Varosha, fenced off from the nearby Turkish Cypriot-populated town of Famagusta.

Three Greek Cypriots civilians and a Turkish Cypriot sentry died last year in intercommunal clashes along the U.N.-patrolled Green Line that runs through the island. It was the heaviest death toll in political violence since 1974.
"This is our front line with the Greek Cypriots," said a young Turkish army captain in Varosha, pointing towards the Greek Cypriot town of Dherinia a few miles (km) away.

He told journalists taken on a restricted tour of Varosha on Thursday that workers were sweeping the streets in an annual clean up. But Turkish Cypriot reporters said street cleaning was unprecedented and could be preparation for settlement.
Turkey stopped short of populating Varosha in 1974 both to keep it as a bargaining chip for later talks and so as not to anger foreign multinationals with big investments in the town.

The United Nations says the town has been looted several times. Many of the windows in its 45 hotels are broken. U.N. estimates in 1994 put the cost of making Varosha habitable again at $500 million over a two-year period.

There would also be a political cost for the Turkish Cypriots, already shunned by most of the world. "If we open Maras we are challenging the whole world, not just the Greeks and Greek Cypriots," said leftist leader Mehmet Ali Talat.
